steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have React and useState available to use in your component.
successCriteria: The import statement should bring in React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'. Check your import statement syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to write an import statement that brings in React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns JSX. Use TypeScript syntax and ensure it returns a JSX element.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function. Make sure to import React if needed for JSX.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns JSX.
successCriteria: Uses TypeScript syntax (explicit return type or inference)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component with proper TypeScript syntax.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure the component is named App and returns JSX (like a div or other element).
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component isn't defined correctly. Check that you've created a function named App that returns JSX.

steps.title: Initialize count state in App
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'count' initialized to 0.
steps.hint: Call useState with the initial value 0 and destructure the returned array into two variables: count and setCount.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a state variable
const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a count state variable that starts at 0 and can be updated later.
successCriteria: The code must include a useState call with initial value 0, destructured into variables named count and setCount.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the count state variable with useState. This gives you a reactive value that can trigger re-renders when updated.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've: 1) Called useState with 0 as the initial value, 2) Used TypeScript generics <number> for the state type, and 3) Destructured the result into [count, setCount].
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on just initializing the count state. Use useState<number>(0) inside the App component and destructure it into [count, setCount].

steps.title: Define increment handler in App
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, define a function named handleIncrement that increases the count state by 1.
steps.hint: Create a function that calls setCount with the current count plus 1.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now has a handleIncrement function that updates the count state.
successCriteria: A function named handleIncrement is defined inside App that calls setCount to increment count by 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the increment handler. This function will be used later to update the count state when a button is clicked.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your function correctly increments the count. Make sure it uses setCount with the current count plus 1.
steps.feedbackWrong: The increment handler isn't defined correctly. Inside the App component, create a function named handleIncrement that calls setCount to increase count by 1.

steps.title: Add button to App that increments count
steps.instruction: Add a button element inside the App component's return statement. The button should have an onClick handler that calls the increment function (which you'll define in the next step). For now, just add the button with an empty onClick handler.
steps.hint: Add a <button> element inside the <div>. Use onClick={} with a placeholder function for now.
steps.expectedOutcome: A button element appears in the App component's JSX, ready to be wired to the increment handler.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a button element with an onClick handler. In the next step, you'll define the actual increment function to connect to it.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added a button element with an onClick attribute inside the App component's return statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Add a button element inside the App component's return statement. The button should have an onClick attribute (you can use a placeholder function for now).

steps.title: Create a Child component without memo
steps.instruction: Create a new functional component named Child that takes a message prop (typed as string) and returns a paragraph displaying that message. Place this component after the App component but before the export default App line.
steps.hint: Define a new function called Child that accepts props with a message property. Use TypeScript to type the message prop as string, then return JSX containing a paragraph element showing the message.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new Child component is defined that accepts a message prop and displays it in a paragraph. This component is not yet used anywhere, but will be used in later steps to demonstrate React.memo.
successCriteria: The code should contain a new component named Child that takes a typed message prop and returns a paragraph element containing that message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a Child component that accepts a typed message prop and displays it. This component will be used to demonstrate how React.memo prevents unnecessary re-renders.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a component, but it might be missing something. Make sure your Child component accepts a message prop typed as string and returns a paragraph element containing that message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Child component isn't defined correctly. Create a new function called Child that takes a message prop (typed as string) and returns a paragraph displaying that message.

steps.title: Add Child component to App with static prop
steps.instruction: Inside the App component's return statement, add the Child component with a static message prop like 'Hello from parent!'
steps.hint: Add <Child message="Hello from parent!" /> somewhere inside the div in App's return statement.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Child component will appear in the App's UI with the static message prop passed to it.
successCriteria: The Child component is rendered inside App's JSX with a static string prop named 'message'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the Child component to App with a static prop. This will allow us to observe how React.memo affects re-renders.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're adding the Child component inside App's return statement with a message prop like message="Hello from parent!". The prop name should be 'message'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Child component needs to be added to App's JSX with a static message prop. Look for where to add it in the return statement.

steps.title: Observe re-renders by adding console.log to Child
steps.instruction: Add a console.log statement inside the Child component to log when it renders.
steps.hint: Place console.log('Child rendered') at the beginning of the Child component function body.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Child component will log 'Child rendered' to the console each time it renders.
successCriteria: The Child component contains a console.log statement that logs a message when the component renders.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added console.log to the Child component. Now you'll be able to see in the console when it re-renders.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added console.log inside the Child component function body.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Child component doesn't have a console.log statement. Add console.log('Child rendered') at the beginning of the Child component function.

steps.title: Import React.memo from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import the memo higher-order component from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Add an import statement that includes memo alongside your existing imports from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing memo from 'react'
import React, { useState, memo } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The memo function is imported from 'react' and available for use.
successCriteria: memo is imported alongside existing imports
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported memo from 'react'. This higher-order component will help optimize your Child component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing memo from the 'react' package alongside your existing imports.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check your import statement. You need to import memo from 'react' to use React.memo.

steps.title: Wrap Child component with React.memo
steps.instruction: Wrap the existing Child component with React.memo to memoize it.
steps.hint: Use React.memo(Child) to create a memoized version of the component.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of wrapping a component with React.memo
const MemoizedComponent = React.memo(Component);
steps.expectedOutcome: The Child component is now memoized using React.memo, which will prevent unnecessary re-renders when its props don't change.
successCriteria: The Child component is wrapped with React.memo
The memoized component is exported or assigned to a variable
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wrapped the Child component with React.memo. This will prevent unnecessary re-renders when the parent component updates but the Child's props remain the same.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're properly wrapping the Child component with React.memo. The syntax should be something like `const MemoizedChild = React.memo(Child);` or `export default React.memo(Child);`.
steps.feedbackWrong: It looks like you haven't wrapped the Child component with React.memo. Remember that React.memo is a higher-order component that takes a component and returns a memoized version of it.

steps.title: Observe reduced re-renders after memo
steps.instruction: Run the application and check the browser console to confirm that the Child component only renders once, even when you click the increment button multiple times.
steps.hint: Open your browser's developer tools (F12 or right-click → Inspect) and look at the Console tab. Click the increment button several times and observe that 'Child rendered' only appears once.
steps.expectedOutcome: The console shows 'Child rendered' only once on initial render, demonstrating that React.memo prevents unnecessary re-renders when props don't change.
successCriteria: The learner should run the app, open the browser console, click the increment button multiple times, and observe that 'Child rendered' appears only once in the console output.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully observed that React.memo prevents unnecessary re-renders. The Child component only renders once because its props don't change, even though the parent App component re-renders on each button click.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to check the browser console after clicking the increment button multiple times. The 'Child rendered' message should appear only once, not on every click.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's check: 1) Did you run the application? 2) Did you open the browser console (F12 or right-click → Inspect → Console)? 3) Did you click the increment button multiple times? You should see 'Child rendered' appear only once in the console.
